V2V OS (1.6.0 to 1.7.2): led the design of the product that moves guests from VMware onto SMTX OS, and between SMTX OS clusters. Snapshot transfer over VMware CBT, a Python control plane, a C core shipped as a shared library. Now on 10,000+ production VMs, including core financial workloads.

[VMTools](https://www.smartx.com/blog/2025/11/elf-vmtools-en/): rebuilt the in-guest agent, which ran operations as shell scripts through QGA guest-exec and leaked zombies on several guest OSes. Filesystem-consistent snapshots: made snapshots filesystem-consistent, not only crash-consistent. The control plane runs fsfreeze in the guest through VMTools before the snapshot, and thaws after.
chunks.resume-en#4:
Cross-cluster live migration: helped build live migration between SMTX OS clusters, and wrote the data check that a libvirt hook fires once it lands. It snapshots both disks through the storage API, then hashes and compares them block by block. Each side holds its compare order in a sequence queue, and the check never blocks switchover.

Guest kernel defects: found with strace a UOS kernel that creates pidfds but never reaps them, hanging customer VMs. The defect went out as a financial-sector advisory and the fix drew a written commendation. Separately rootcaused old kernels not re-polling the QGA serial fd, which silently truncated host-to-guest JSON.

chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#0:
Copy-as-Decode: Grammar-Constrained Parallel
Prefill for LLM Editing

Ziyang Liu
Independent Researcher
ziyang.liu.r@outlook.com
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#1:
Large language models edit text and code by autoregressively regenerating the
full output, even when most tokens appear verbatim in the input. We study a
decoding-layer mechanism, Copy-as-Decode, that recasts edit generation as structured decoding over a two-primitive grammar—<copy lines="i-j"/> references
an input line range, <gen> ... </gen> emits new content. A token-level FSM
guarantees syntactic validity, and a serving-layer primitive updates the KV cache
for each copy span via a single parallel-prefill forward rather than N autoregressive
steps, sharing the parallel-forward kernel of speculative decoding but with input
tokens as the draft and program-enforced acceptance in place of probabilistic verification. The contribution is the mechanism together with an upper-bound analysis
of its payoff that requires no end-to-end model training.
We report two quantitative bounds and one correctness property. (i) Kernel
speedup: on Qwen2.5-{1.5B, 7B}, copying N tokens via parallel prefill is 6.8×–
303× faster than emitting them autoregressively (N ∈ [8, 512], A100 80GB bf16).
(ii) Copy ceiling: on ProbeEdit and HumanEvalPack-Fix (Py/JS), 74–98% of gold
tokens are reachable under the line-level primitive; composed with the empirical
kernel s(N ) over each corpus’s exact span histogram this yields the closed-form
wall-clock bound bndexact = 29.0 × /3.4 × /4.2× (ProbeEdit / Py / JS; 13.0×
pooled). A token-level extension reaches 91–99% coverage with conservative
floors of 4.5–6.5×. (iii) Pipeline losslessness: oracle programs round-trip through
the deterministic resolver on all 482 cases, an identifiability precondition that
localizes any downstream failure to span selection rather than the mechanism.
A perturbation study shows pooled EM drops from 100% to 15.48% under offby-one noise, quantifying the span-selection precision required. A supervised
fine-tuning pilot on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (131–385 oracle programs, 3 seeds, 99
held-out attempts per configuration) lifts HEvalFix-Py EM from 0/33 (untrained,
any strategy) to 12–17% (Wilson 95% CI [7.0, 26.0]), a learnability signal, not a
production-accuracy span selector. We do not claim batched-serving integration or
agentic multi-file coverage; these are scoped as direct follow-up.
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#3:
LLM-based editing of text and code is pervasive—code-assistant apply loops, notebook rewrites,
collaborative document revision—yet the dominant serving strategy is wasteful. Given an input
document D and an instruction, the model emits the edited output D′ autoregressively, one token
at a time, from scratch. Because typical edits preserve most of D verbatim (e.g. 74–98% of gold
tokens reproducible from D under our line-level copy primitive, §4.2), most of those forward passes
regenerate content the model has already attended to in its prompt. This has two compounding costs:
wall-clock latency scales with output length, not with edit size, and the model is free to drift on tokens
that should have been fixed by the edit contract.
Preprint. Under review.
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#4:
![Figure 1: Mechanism comparison. (a) Standard autoregressive decoding spends one forward pass per output token. (b) Speculative decoding uses a small draft model](/corpus/figures/copy-as-decode-002-000.jpg)
Figure 1: Mechanism comparison. (a) Standard autoregressive decoding spends one forward pass
per output token. (b) Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose k tokens that the target
model verifies in one parallel forward; tokens are accepted probabilistically. (c) Copy-as-Decode
degenerates the draft to the input document: a grammar-constrained decoder commits to a specific
<copy lines="i-j"/> span, and one parallel-prefill forward splices the corresponding N input
tokens into the KV cache with acceptance = 1 by construction. The kernel operation in (c) is the same
parallel forward used in (b)’s verifier, but with zero rejection risk inside a copy op. Full mechanism
in §2.
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#5:
Scope of this paper. We study a decoding-layer mechanism, not a production editing system.
We (a) formulate the mechanism, (b) establish two quantitative upper bounds and one correctness
property—composed into a single span-distribution-aware exact bound bndexact (Table 2) that
holds independently of base-model quality, (c) characterize, via a controlled perturbation study,
the span-selection precision a downstream trained system would need to realize those bounds, and
(d) run a small-scale SFT pilot (§5) that reaches 12–17% mean-over-3-seeds held-out EM (95%
CI [7.0, 20.1] and [11.0, 26.0] respectively) at 1.5B on 131–385 examples—clearing the untrained
0% baseline decisively but below deployment. We do not integrate the splice with batched-serving
stacks (vLLM/SGLang) or evaluate on agentic multi-file workloads (SWE-bench-style); our endto-end spot-check on a 7B untrained base (Appendix P) places the current model relative to the
oracle ceiling but is not itself the efficiency claim. Prior work addresses edit serving only partly.
Search-and-replace formats [6] and unified diffs reduce output tokens but still re-emit structural
context through autoregressive decoding, and suffer anchor-ambiguity failures we quantify in §4.4
(search/replace round-trip-EM drops to 0.81–0.94 on our corpora where C OPY- AS -D ECODE remains
at 1.00). Speculative decoding [1, 13, 14, 28] accelerates free-form generation with probabilistic
acceptance but offers no token-identity guarantees on copy-heavy regions; production apply tools [4]
are trained on proprietary data and not directly reproducible. We take a simpler view: if 90%+ of
output tokens are a priori present as contiguous input spans, the act of copying them should not cost
the same as the act of generating new ones. Concretely:
Grammar over two primitives. We replace free-form output with a programmatic grammar
program := ’<program>’ (copy | gen)* ’</program>’
copy := ’<copy lines="i-j"/>’
gen := ’<gen>’ free_text ’</gen>’
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#6:
enforced by a token-level finite-state machine that restricts the model’s logits to tokens whose
decoded prefix is consistent with the current grammar state. The decoder has three branches at each
op boundary (start a copy, start a gen, end the program); inside a copy op the model picks only the
numeric line indices; inside a gen op the model runs free until </gen>. The grammar guarantees
100% parse rate by construction.
Copy spans cost one parallel prefill. After the model commits to <copy lines="i-j"/>, the
tokens for lines i..j are already known—they are literal tokens from the input. We splice them into
the output sequence and update the KV cache with a single parallel-prefill forward, skipping N
autoregressive decode steps for a span of N tokens. This shares the parallel-forward acceleration
primitive of speculative decoding [1, 13, 25] but replaces probabilistic verification with grammar2
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#7:
enforced acceptance: input tokens serve as the “draft” with acceptance probability 1 by construction.

The quality trade-off lives entirely in span selection.

Two quantitative bounds + one correctness property, without end-to-end training.

The mechanism decomposes into three independently measurable properties.

Two are quantitative bounds
on the payoff any copy-aware decoder can achieve (kernel speedup and copy ceiling); the third is a
correctness precondition, not an independent bound (pipeline losslessness—without it an EM failure
cannot be attributed to span selection).

Composed, the first two yield the span-distribution-aware
exact bound bndexact (Table 2) that defines the payoff envelope any future trained system would have
to fit inside.

None of the three requires training a span selector.

1.

Kernel speedup (§4.1).

For spans of length 8–512 and a 1024-token prefix on Qwen2.5-1.5B /
7B (single-sequence A100 80GB bf16), a parallel-prefill forward is 6.8×–303× faster than an
autoregressive loop over the same tokens.

Speedup grows approximately linearly with span length
in the overhead-dominated regime and saturates at the compute-bound regime.

2.

Copy ceiling (§4.2).

For ProbeEdit (154 short-text edits) and HumanEvalPack-Fix (164 Python
+ 164 JS bug fixes), 74–98% of gold-output tokens are realizable as contiguous line-level copy
spans under oracle alignment—the ceiling for the mechanism as defined in §2.

Composed with the
measured kernel s(N ) curve over each corpus’s actual span histogram, this yields the exact closedform wall-clock bound bndexact = 29.0× (ProbeEdit), 3.4× (HEvalFix-Py), 4.2× (HEvalFix-JS),
13.0× pooled.

A token-level contiguous-span cover (an aspirational upper bound, not the current
primitive) reaches 91–99% with conservative floors at 4.5–6.5×, motivating the natural extension
to sub-line copy discussed in §7.

3.

Pipeline losslessness (§4.3).

With oracle programs induced from difflib.SequenceMatcher
alignment of gold to input, the deterministic resolver reproduces gold on all 482 cases across three
corpora under byte-equal comparison (up to a single trailing newline); whitespace-trimmed EM is
also 482/482.

This is an identifiability precondition, not a payoff bound: any downstream exactmatch failure is therefore a model span-selection problem, not a mechanism bug.

A perturbation
study (Table 8) shows the mechanism is unforgiving: pooled EM drops from 100% to 15.48%
under off-by-one noise on oracle line indices.
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#8:
Kernel speedup and copy ceiling are systems and data properties that do not depend on model quality;
pipeline losslessness establishes that the resolver faithfully inverts an oracle program.

Closing the
gap between the oracle ceiling and a realized deployed system is a model-training question—picking
the right spans—that we scope as follow-up work (§7).

The perturbation study in §5 quantifies how
tight that selector has to be; it is a hardness diagnosis, not itself a feasibility result.

A prompt-level
variant of the grammar (the only contribution of the paper superseded by this one, CRP) is retained as
an ablation for closed-model deployment without KV-cache access (Appendix Q).

chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#9:
Copy-as-Decode sits at the intersection of structured constrained decoding and speculative decoding
(Figure 1). The mechanism has three components—a two-primitive grammar, a token-level finitestate machine that enforces it, and a parallel-prefill splice that realizes a copy span in one forward
pass—each introduced below.
2.1

Grammar and Problem Formulation

Given an input document D = l1 l2 · · · ln (indexed by lines) and an edit instruction I, the goal is to
produce the edited document D′ . Rather than autoregressively generating D′ token by token, we
have the model emit a program over a two-primitive grammar:
Program ::= <program> Op∗ </program>
Op ::= Copy | Gen
Copy ::= <copy lines="i-j"/>
Gen ::= <gen> F REE T EXT </gen>
A deterministic resolver R consumes a Program P and the immutable input D, and yields D′ =
R(P, D). Line indices reference the original D (no renumbering after edits).

Resolver Semantics

The resolver is deterministic and pure:

chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#12:
1. For each <copy lines="i-j"/> op, emit the verbatim text of li · · · lj from D, joined by newlines.
2. For each <gen>s</gen> op, emit s with at most one leading and one trailing newline stripped (a
readability allowance, preserving internal blank lines).
3. Concatenate ops with a single newline separator.
The resolver’s default behavior on out-of-range or malformed indices is to raise, but a single flag
toggles between strict (raise on any malformed op) and clipped (clip indices to [1, n], emit a warning)
semantics—we benchmark both modes explicitly in Table 4. It has no nondeterminism and no
dependence on the model. §4.3 measures pipeline losslessness: on all 482 (doc, gold) pairs across
three corpora, oracle programs induced from line-level alignment reconstruct gold exactly under strict
semantics—the strict-vs-clipped distinction matters only at deployment under a model that can emit
invalid indices, not for the oracle-derivation pipeline itself.
Reserved literals and principled escape. The grammar’s five structural substrings (<copy,
</copy>, <gen>, </gen>, </program>) must not appear verbatim inside a <gen>-body. We handle
this in two complementary places:
• Preprocessing escape. Each reserved substring in gold is replaced by a Unicode entity (e.g.
</gen>→〈/gen〉 via U+27E8/U+27E9/U+2024, unused by all tokenizers we checked); resolver
reverses before emit. For any gold g, decode(encode(g)) = g and encode is injective on inputs
free of the entities—holds on 482/482 cases and 10,000 adversarial fuzz strings (Appendix I).
• FSM end-of-gen detector. Exact token-id-sequence match against the 3-token Qwen BPE encoding
of </gen>, not a substring check on decoded text. Byte-level overlaps split across token boundaries
cannot mis-trigger the detector (Appendix I).
2.3
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#13:
Token-Level Grammar-Constrained Decoder

A free-form decoder cannot be trusted to emit a valid Program: after a copy-span splice it has
just “seen itself output” a long run of document-like tokens and naturally continues regenerating
content. We enforce the grammar at the token level via a small FSM (5 states: AWAIT_OP, AFTER_LT,
COPY_LINES, GEN_BODY, CLOSE; see Appendix A) that intersects the model’s logits with the set of
tokens consistent with the current state. For Qwen2.5-family tokenizers (and any BPE tokenizer
encoding the structural literals as fixed token sequences), the relevant token ids are fixed constants.
The FSM alternates three step types:
• Masked model steps at decision points: argmax restricted to {<, </} at op boundaries; {copy, gen}
for op type; digits plus -/" inside a copy’s line range.
• Forced-template prefills for fixed literal sequences (_lines=", "/>, </gen>, </program>), each
spliced via a single parallel-prefill forward.
• Free generation inside <gen> bodies until the 3-token Qwen encoding of </gen> is produced
(Appendix I).
The structural portion is therefore never subject to model error; the model chooses only op types, line
indices, and <gen>-body content. Parse rate is 100% by construction.
2.4

Copy-Span Splicing via Parallel Prefill
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#14:
When the FSM exits the copy-line-index state with a chosen range [i, j], we tokenize li · · · lj directly
from D and append those tokens to the KV cache in a single forward pass:
model(input_ids = [[li · · · lj ]], past_key_values = KV)
This is an ordinary transformer prefill forward over N = |[[li · · · lj ]]| tokens, not N decode forwards.
The forward still computes all self-attention and feed-forward activations over the N tokens, but
it does so in parallel within one launch, amortizing the per-step kernel overhead and, on modern
hardware, running in the GEMM-bound regime rather than the memory-bandwidth-bound regime
typical of single-token decode.
Copy-as-Decode shares the parallel-forward acceleration primitive of speculative decoding [1, 13,

chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#28:
Oracle programs are derived by deterministic difflib.SequenceMatcher line-level alignment (no
model) and resolved through the same code path invoked at deployment. Reconstruction is byte-exact
on all 482/482 cases across ProbeEdit (154), HEvalFix-Py (164), and HEvalFix-JS (164), under both
byte-exact (tolerant of a single trailing newline) and trimmed (.strip()) equality. A grammar-literal
audit finds 0/482 gold outputs containing the reserved substrings </gen> or <copy. This establishes:
(i) the resolver is lossless on all cases up to at most a single trailing newline; (ii) any downstream
exact-match failure decomposes as span-selection error, not resolver error; (iii) the naive grammar
suffices on these corpora, though general-purpose deployment requires the principled escape of §2.2.

Aider-style apply rewrites the first match and produces a wrong edit. Unified diff avoids this by

The key qualitative point: even before decoding speedup, the decoding cost under C OPY- AS D ECODE is already a strict improvement on the incumbent format-cost Pareto frontier. Search/replace
matches our token budget on two of three corpora but at a fidelity cost (anchor ambiguity); unified
diff matches our fidelity but costs 17–64% more tokens. Layering the KV-splice kernel (§4.1) on top
of C OPY- AS -D ECODE’s token-budget advantage is what drives the end-to-end speedup discussed
next.

Span-selection brittleness.

Perfect line-level span selection round-trips to gold on all 482 oracle
cases (§4.3); how tight must a realized selector be?

We perturb each oracle CopyLines endpoint by
integer noise ∼ Uniform[−ϵ, +ϵ], clamp to the valid document range, and re-run the resolver.

Figure 6 shows the collapse is sharp: at ϵ=1 (each line index off by at most one line) trimmed EM
drops from 100% to 9–25% across corpora.

Line-level addressing is an unforgiving representation—
small index errors do not produce small output errors—unlike token-matching apply tools where
a near-match on the anchor still localizes the edit.

A deployed selector must achieve near-perfect
per-copy endpoint accuracy to realize the oracle ceiling; the 100% → 9–25% gap at ϵ=1 is the
operational target any subsequent span-selection training must hit.

Pointer-decoder baseline. A natural architectural alternative is a span-level pointer decoder [26]:
attach three classification heads to a base LM (op-type, span-start, span-end), training end-to-end to
emit the same {COPY, GEN} op sequence without serializing through XML text. The information
content per COPY op is identical—two small integers—so selector-EM should match C OPY- AS D ECODE. Where they differ is fixed cost per op: a span-level pointer pays 3 autoregressive forward
passes (op-type+start+end), while C OPY- AS -D ECODE pays 2 (FSM open/close) + 1 (forced template
prefill) + N/s(N ) (parallel-prefill splice) = 3 + N/s(N ). The pointer is therefore strictly cheaper
in fixed overhead (by ≈ 0.15 forward-pass-equivalents per copy op on our corpora; see Appendix L),
but requires dedicated training and dedicated heads, while C OPY- AS -D ECODE is a format layered
on any instruction-tuned LM. A token-level pointer (predict input-position at every copied token) is
strictly dominated: N forward passes vs N/s(N ). The mechanism claim is thus not “copy is free”—a
span-level pointer achieves that with architectural surgery—but “copy can be made format-level and
still get most of the way there,” which is the deployable property.
Composition with speculative decoding. The splice accelerates copy regions; speculative decoding [13, 14] accelerates generation regions. The two are orthogonal and compose multiplicatively.
Under the extended cost model (Appendix H), a gen region of n tokens costs 2 + n AR steps without
speculation and 2 + n/sspec with; copy regions are unaffected. Using the measured Qwen2.5-7B
splice curve (Table 11) and a conservative sspec =2.5× (middle of the 2–3× range typically reported
on code [14]), the combined predicted speedup over full regeneration rises from 22.4× to 27.1× on
ProbeEdit (copy-heavy), 2.8× to 3.4× on HEvalFix-Py (gen-heavy small fixes), and 4.4× to 5.9×

work and report the ceiling here as the ceiling C OPY- AS -D ECODE’s mechanism admits.
What this does not establish. At 14–17% EM the pilot is below any production threshold. It
demonstrates learnability of the line-level representation at commodity scale and portability of the
gain across two languages and one text corpus (within ±3 pp; Appendix O), not a deployable system.
The closed-model prompt-level variant (§Q) reaches 80% EM on GPT-5-mini, upper-bounding what a
constrained-decoding variant on a comparable-capability base can achieve when the FSM additionally

Speculative decoding and draft-based acceleration. Blockwise parallel decoding [25] first observed that a single parallel forward can verify multiple draft tokens at once; speculative decoding [3, 13, 28] generalized this with a draft-model/target-model distinction and a probabilistic
acceptance rule that preserves the target distribution. Medusa [1] replaces the separate draft model
with extra prediction heads on the target; EAGLE [14, 15] drafts in feature space rather than token
space; SpecInfer [19] extends to tree-based draft expansion; Yang et al. [29], Zhang et al. [30] explore
multi-candidate and self-drafting variants; REST [10] retrieves drafts from a corpus. Across this
family, drafts are produced by some learned predictor and accepted probabilistically to preserve the
target distribution.
Copy-as-Decode shares the parallel-forward primitive but differs in two architectural respects: the
“draft” is the input document (not a smaller-model prediction) selected by grammar commitment, and
acceptance is unconditional (not probabilistic)—so Copy-as-Decode does not preserve speculative
decoding’s free-form target distribution, redefining the decoded task as an edit program. In exchange
it avoids draft-model training and obtains a trivial parallel-forward ratio equal to the AR-vs-PP kernel
ratio. The two methods compose: within a <gen> body, any speculative-decoding scheme can further
accelerate free-text generation.
Prompt-lookup decoding and input-aware drafting. The closest prior mechanism is promptlookup decoding [22]: draft candidate continuations by suffix-matching against the prompt and

Edit-as-program paradigms. Casting editing as emitting a program over the input has precedent
outside decoder-accelerated serving; they differ in granularity and in whether the program is applied
at decode-time or post-decode:
• String-level: search/replace (Aider [6]) and unified-diff apply.
• Per-token tag: LaserTagger [18], FELIX [17], GECToR [21].
• Prompt-level line-reference: CRP [16].
• Decode-time line-reference, KV-splicing (ours): Copy-as-Decode.
What distinguishes this work is the coupling between program form and serving primitive: the
line-reference program is chosen so the deterministic resolver realizes as a parallel-prefill KV-cache
splice over the model’s own KV, not a post-decode string application. The format-cost head-to-head
of Table 3 and the kernel measurement of Figure 3 are the two halves of this coupling; no prior
edit-as-program paradigm offers the second half.
Deterministic KV splicing: prior attempts. We are aware of no prior mechanism that splices
input-token KV segments into a decoder’s KV cache with deterministic (unconditional) acceptance
during autoregressive decoding. Table 10 positions the closest candidates.

Constrained decoding. Structured constrained decoding enforces an output grammar at the token
level: PICARD [23] monitors partial SQL for well-formedness; Outlines [27] formulates decoding
as finite-state intersection by compiling regular expressions and context-free grammars into tokenlevel FSMs with a vocabulary index; XGrammar [5] and SGLang [31] provide efficient parallel-safe
grammar compilation; Geng et al. [7] extends this to unconstrained LMs by masking with EBNF/CFG
grammars without fine-tuning. Our FSM (§2.3) is a small instance of this family: an FSM over the
16
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#52:
<copy>/<gen> grammar, made efficient by exploiting that Qwen-family BPE tokenizers encode each
structural literal as a fixed multi-token sequence.

What is distinctive is not the FSM itself but that the
FSM serves a dual role—guaranteeing parse rate and marking the points at which the parallel-prefill
splice can be invoked.

Grammar-engine masking overhead.

A parallel line of systems work focuses on driving per-step
mask construction near zero: XGrammar [5] compiles a context-free grammar into an adaptive
token-mask cache; SGLang [31] amortizes mask computation across requests via runtime sharing.

Our FSM sits at the lower bound of this cost spectrum: 5 states, at most 12 allowed token-ids
at any masked step (Figure 7 and Appendix A), measured at cmask = 0.02 ms per masked step
on Qwen2.5-1.5B (Appendix H)—two orders of magnitude below a single decode step.

Copy-asDecode’s grammar-constrained path is therefore compatible with any of the above engines and adds
no measurable masking overhead; the substantive cost is the parallel-prefill splice, which none of
these engines provide.

Edit formats and apply models.

Production tools use a variety of output formats for code and
document edits.

Aider [6] uses search/replace blocks, where the model emits both the verbatim text
to find and the verbatim text to replace; unified-diff emits the standard @@ hunk format used by git.

Cursor’s instant-apply [4] and Anthropic’s text-editor tool are closed-model apply pipelines whose
training recipes are not public.

Related work on editing as a task—SWE-bench [11], CanItEdit [2],
HumanEvalPack [20]—evaluates end-to-end correctness rather than the decoding mechanism itself.

All of these require the model to re-emit structural context (search anchors, hunk headers, or the entire
edited span) through ordinary autoregressive decoding.

Copy-as-Decode differs in replacing the
model-produced reference with a grammar-enforced one, and in splicing the referenced tokens into
the KV cache rather than paying decode cost for them.

§4.4 benchmarks these formats head-to-head
on a unified parse+apply harness: search/replace matches our format-theoretic token budget but loses
6–19% of cases to anchor ambiguity, while unified diff matches our round-trip fidelity but costs
17–64% more tokens per edit.

Copy mechanisms at the architectural level.

Pointer networks [26] and copy mechanisms [8, 24]
augment encoder-decoder generation with a learned pointer distribution over input positions.
chunks.paper-copy-as-decode#53:
Edit-astagging architectures—LaserTagger [18], FELIX [17], GECToR [21]—cast editing as classifying
each input token with an operation.

The Levenshtein Transformer [9] learns non-autoregressive
insertion/deletion operations.

These approaches modify the model itself.

Copy-as-Decode instead
operates at the decoding and serving layer: any pretrained autoregressive LM that can be coaxed to
emit the <copy>/<gen> grammar under the FSM can be served with it.

Prompt-level structured output for edits.

Closed-model structured-output prompting [16] has
been studied as an edit format—the model emits a line-referencing program that a deterministic
resolver expands.

Our earlier work on CRP falls in this category; we treat it here as the prompt-level
variant of Copy-as-Decode (Appendix Q) that retains the output-token compression benefit but not
the wall-clock kernel speedup.

The mechanism-level contribution of this paper is the combination of
grammar-constrained decoding, parallel-prefill splicing, and a lossless resolver.

We recast edit generation as structured decoding over a two-primitive grammar, enforced by a tokenlevel FSM and accelerated by a parallel-prefill splice that replaces N autoregressive decode steps
with one forward. The contribution is the mechanism together with three measurable properties—two
quantitative bounds and one correctness property—independent of model quality: (i) one parallelprefill forward is 6.8×–303× faster than N autoregressive decodes for N ∈ [8, 512] on Qwen2.5{1.5B, 7B}; (ii) 74–98% of gold tokens are realizable under the line-level primitive on ProbeEdit
and HumanEvalPack-Fix, which composed with the kernel curve over each corpus’s exact span
histogram yields the closed-form wall-clock bound bndexact = 29.0 × /3.4 × /4.2× (ProbeEdit / Py
/ JS, 13.0× pooled); (iii) oracle programs round-trip byte-exactly on all 482 cases—an identifiability
precondition that localizes any downstream EM failure to span selection. A perturbation study
(pooled EM 100% → 15.48% under off-by-one noise) gives an operational target for any trained
selector.

Scope. In scope: contiguous line-range copy (and, in the token-level extension of §5, contiguous
token-range copy) from a single input document to a single output document, with K ≤ 20 ops per edit
on the evaluated corpora. Out of scope for the present paper: multi-file and agentic workloads (SWEbench-style); AST-granular edits whose operands are subtrees rather than spans; splice integration
into the vLLM/SGLang scheduler (format-only latency gains on vLLM 0.19 continuous batching are
measured in §4.5; paged-attention splice integration is scaffolded in Appendix K and deferred).
Limitations and future work. The FSM’s fixed-id table is tokenizer-conditional and resolved
once at load (Appendix K: ≥ 7/14 of our structural literals are single-token across Qwen2.5,
DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama-family tokenizers; fragmented tokenizers add ≈ 0.02 ms per
literal). Reserved-literal substrings in gold are handled by a principled Unicode-entity escape (§2.2,
I), so “the gold-audit holds on our corpora” is no longer the load-bearing claim. Line granularity
loses coverage to sub-expression rewrites; the 74–98% vs. 93–99% line-vs-token gap (Table 2,
Appendix N) is closed by the token-indexed <copy tokens> primitive, which we formalize and
measure as an oracle-ceiling in this draft but whose realized selector training we defer. The pilot
selector at 14–18% EM is a learnability signal, not a deployment result. Four concrete follow-ups:
(i) scale the selector to 7B QLoRA with larger corpora and span-end-targeted supervision (span-end
accuracy is the dominant error, §5); (ii) productize the token-level <copy tokens> primitive under
a trained selector; (iii) integrate the splice into vLLM/SGLang continuous batching with paged
attention and report E2E latency/throughput at realistic QPS, above the format-only 2.1–3.3× floor
we measure in §4.5; (iv) apply in code-editing agent loops and on SWE-bench-style benchmarks.

Cooperative Memory Paging with Keyword Bookmarks
for Long-Horizon LLM Conversations
Ziyang Liu
Independent Researcher
ziyang.liu.r@outlook.com
chunks.paper-memory-paging#1:
When LLM conversations grow beyond the
context window, old content must be evicted—
but how does the model recover evicted information when it needs it? Existing approaches
either require the model to self-diagnose information gaps via explicit retrieval calls,
detect faults only for tool outputs like file
reads, or compress content irreversibly. We
propose cooperative paging: evicted conversation segments are replaced with minimal keyword bookmarks ([pN:keywords],
∼8 tokens each), and the model is given a
recall() tool to retrieve full content on demand. The bookmarks serve as a lightweight
table of contents for compressed memory, enabling the model to decide when retrieval
is needed.
On the LoCoMo benchmark
(10 real multi-session conversations, 300+
turns each), cooperative paging achieves the
highest answer quality among six methods
tested—outperforming truncation, BM25 retrieval, word-overlap retrieval, a search-tool
baseline, and truncated full context—on four
models from three provider families (GPT-4omini, DeepSeek-v3.2, Claude Haiku, GLM5), a ranking confirmed by four independent
LLM judges (p=0.017 vs. BM25, paired bootstrap). We then study the paging design space
directly with a turn-by-turn simulator (3,176
probes on synthetic long conversations, 1,600
on LoCoMo): a 5×4 ablation over pageboundary strategies (fixed-size, topic-shift,
exchange-count) and eviction policies (FIFO,
LRU, LFU, Bélády oracle). We find that
(1) page granularity dominates: coarse fixedsize pages (fixed 20) reach 96.7% while
content-aware topic shift over-fragments
and collapses to 56.7%; (2) eviction policies
are data-dependent: Bélády upper-bounds
online policies by 8–14 points, and which
online policy wins flips between forwardmoving synthetic data (FIFO) and revisitheavy LoCoMo (LFU); (3) the bookmark generation bottleneck is partially closable: of six
chunks.paper-memory-paging#2:
bookmark generation strategies we test, two
improve over the heuristic baseline—hybrid
(heuristic + LLM-discriminative augmentation) on synthetic data (+4.4 E2E points) and
llm-batch (single-call cross-page non-overlap)
on real LoCoMo dialogues (+8.7 points, +50
on open-domain questions). The other four
strategies, including TF·IDF and per-page
LLM, under-perform the heuristic by lowering the recall trigger rate—a structural failure mode predicted by the information-gap hypothesis; (4) the bookmark is now the bottleneck: the model triggers recall() 96% of
the time but selects the correct page only 57%
of the time when bookmarks are insufficiently

chunks.paper-memory-paging#3:
Large language models deployed in multi-turn
conversations face a fundamental resource management problem: the context window is finite,
but conversation history grows without bound.
When the context budget is exceeded, old content
must be evicted. The question is: how does the
model get evicted content back when it needs it?
This problem is the memory management problem that operating systems solved decades ago
with virtual memory and demand paging (Denning, 1968). In OS paging, the application is unaware of physical memory limits; the OS transparently loads pages from disk when needed. Recent
work has applied this analogy to LLMs: Packer
et al. (2023) introduced hierarchical memory tiers
with explicit retrieval via function calls, and Mason (2026) built a transparent paging proxy for
agentic coding sessions. However, existing approaches have fundamental limitations. MemGPT
requires the model to self-diagnose information
gaps—but models cannot reliably detect what they
chunks.paper-memory-paging#4:
do not know. Pichay detects faults only through
tool-call matching, which is limited to addressable
outputs like file reads. Compression approaches
like Adaptive Focus Memory (Cruz, 2025) lose
details irreversibly.
We propose cooperative paging: when conversation content is evicted, it is replaced with a minimal keyword bookmark costing only ∼8 tokens,
e.g.:
[p3:

allergy, peanut, budget]
chunks.paper-memory-paging#5:
The model is given a recall() tool to retrieve
the full content of any bookmarked segment on demand. Unlike MemGPT, where the model must
formulate free-form search queries about what it
might be missing, our bookmarks provide a table
of contents for compressed memory: the model
sees which topics are available and decides when
to retrieve. This shifts the cognitive load from
“guess what you might need” to “check the index.”
We evaluate cooperative paging on both controlled experiments and the LoCoMo benchmark
(Maharana et al., 2024)—a dataset of real multisession conversations spanning 300+ turns. Our
contributions are:
1. A cooperative paging mechanism using minimal keyword bookmarks and a recall tool.
On controlled scenarios, the model achieves
91% recall accuracy with zero observed false
positives (n = 22). On LoCoMo, Bookmark+Recall achieves the highest answer quality among six methods on both GPT-4o-mini
and DeepSeek-v3.2 (§4).
2. A paging design study that treats page boundary and eviction policy as first-class design
choices. Using a turn-by-turn paging simulator, we run a full 5×4 ablation (3,176 synthetic
probes, 1,600 LoCoMo probes) and find that
page granularity dominates (fixed-size 96.7%
vs. topic-shift 56.7%), Bélády’s oracle beats
FIFO by 14 points, and the remaining bottleneck has shifted from “when to recall” (now
96% correct) to “which page to recall” (57%
correct). To our knowledge, this is the first
study of page boundary detection and eviction
policies for in-session LLM conversation paging (§5).
3. Design principles for bookmark construction:
minimal keyword bookmarks (∼8–24 tokens)
achieve the best accuracy-to-cost ratio over
richer formats, and keyword specificity is the
chunks.paper-memory-paging#6:
most impactful design factor in our controlled
study, accounting for a 25.7 percentage point
improvement (§6).
4. Closing the bookmark bottleneck.
We
propose two complementary bookmark generation strategies—hybrid (heuristic + LLMdiscriminative augmentation) and llm-batch
(single-call cross-page non-overlap)—that improve end-to-end accuracy by +4.4 points on
synthetic data and +8.7 points on real LoCoMo
dialogues, with a +50 point improvement on
open-domain questions. Critically, four other
natural strategies (TF·IDF, per-page LLM, etc.)
under-perform the heuristic baseline by lowering the recall trigger rate—a structural failure
mode we link back to the information-gap hypothesis (§7).

2

Why Passive Fault Detection Fails

2.1

Hypothesis

A natural approach to detecting memory faults is
to monitor the model’s output uncertainty. When
generating a response, if the model needs information that was evicted, its token-level NLL should
spike—analogous to a hardware page fault in OS
virtual memory. EM-LLM (Fountas et al., 2025)
demonstrated that Bayesian surprise (a form of
prediction error) effectively segments input text
into episodic events. We hypothesized that the
same signal, applied during output generation,
could detect when the model lacks evicted context.
2.2

chunks.paper-memory-paging#10:
The root cause is that models do not “struggle”
when lacking context. Instead, they generate
a different response—one that is simpler, more
generic, and often more confident. When the
model knows about a peanut allergy, it generates
cautious restaurant recommendations with hedging language (higher NLL). Without this knowledge, it recommends restaurants directly and fluently (lower NLL). A confident wrong answer has
low NLL.
Design implication. This pilot suggests that
NLL-based uncertainty signals are not a reliable
basis for detecting memory faults in LLMs—at
least under gist compression with GPT-4o-mini.
The underlying issue is that models do not “struggle” when lacking context; they simply produce a
different, often more confident, response. While a
more exhaustive study (more models, more compression regimes, alternative uncertainty signals)
could refine this picture, the failure mode is fundamental enough to motivate a cooperative design:
the system should explicitly inform the model
about what was compressed, rather than hoping
to detect information gaps from output behavior
alone.

chunks.paper-memory-paging#11:
OS-Inspired LLM Memory. The analogy between context windows and physical memory has
motivated several systems. Kwon et al. (2023)
apply OS paging to KV cache management at
the hardware level. Packer et al. (2023) propose MemGPT, which organizes LLM memory
into hierarchical tiers (main context, recall storage, archival storage) and uses function calls for
retrieval. Mason (2026) build Pichay, a transparent
proxy that implements demand paging for agentic
context windows, detecting page faults via toolcall matching. Our work differs in two ways: we
operate on conversation content rather than tool
outputs, and we use cooperative bookmarks rather
than requiring explicit retrieval calls or tool-call
matching.
Context Compression and Truncation.
StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2024) maintains
a sliding window with attention sinks, discarding middle content permanently. Infini-attention
(Munkhdalai et al., 2024) compresses past context
into a fixed-size memory matrix. LLMLingua
(Jiang et al., 2023) and Selective Context (Li
et al., 2023) prune low-information tokens. Adaptive Focus Memory (Cruz, 2025) assigns each
message one of three fidelity levels (full, compressed, placeholder) under a token budget. These
approaches perform irreversible compression—
once details are lost, they cannot be recovered.
Our bookmark mechanism is reversible: the
recall() tool restores full content from external storage.
Episodic and Retrieval-Based Memory. EMLLM (Fountas et al., 2025) uses surprise-based
segmentation inspired by human episodic memory
to organize tokens into coherent events, achieving strong performance on long-context benchmarks. ReadAgent (Lee et al., 2024) applies
episode pagination with gist memory for long document comprehension. Mem0 (Chhikara et al.,
2025) and A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025) build pro-

chunks.paper-memory-paging#13:
Our approach replaces evicted conversation segments with minimal keyword bookmarks and provides a recall() tool for on-demand retrieval.
Figure 2 illustrates the full pipeline.
Segmentation. Conversation turns are grouped
into pages of 5 turns each. When the context budget is exceeded, the oldest pages are compressed.
Bookmark generation. Each compressed page
is replaced with a keyword bookmark:

Keywords are extracted automatically from page
content using a simple heuristic: capitalized multicharacter tokens, numbers, and dates from the
first 3–4 turns of each page, filtered against a 60word stopword list and limited to 3–5 keywords.
No manual curation, LLM calls, or conversationtype-specific rules are used—the same extraction
pipeline runs identically for all conversation types.
Each bookmark costs ∼8–24 tokens (depending
on keyword count and format syntax), compared
to ∼200–500 tokens for the original page content.

• Synthetic long conversations (20 conversations, 120–200 turns each). Each conversation
contains 6–8 planted facts from 8 categories (allergy, budget, contact, deadline, medical, number, preference, schedule), with probe questions
interspersed throughout and re-probed at the

• LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), where we

This tests our paging design on real, humangenerated dialogue.
Strategies. We compare five page boundary
strategies and four eviction policies in a full
cross. Boundaries: fixed 5, fixed 10, and
fixed 20 split every N turns; topic shift
splits when the Jaccard word-overlap between the
previous 5 turns and the new turn drops below
0.15; exchange 5 splits after five user–assistant
exchanges. Eviction: FIFO (oldest first), LRU
(evict the page whose content was least recently
referenced by a probe or recall; updated at each
probe), LFU (evict the page with the fewest cumulative references; ties broken by age), and Bélády
(oracle: evict the page whose next use is furthest
in the future). Bélády upper-bounds what any online policy can achieve (Belády, 1966). Recalled
pages are returned to the active set for one probe
and then re-evicted.
We report recall accuracy: a probe is correct if
either (a) the needed page is still active at probe
time, or (b) the model calls recall() with the
correct page id. Full-grid runs total 3,176 probes
on synthetic data and 1,600 probes on LoCoMo.

7

Closing the Bookmark Bottleneck

Section 5 identified a sharp asymmetry in cooperative paging: the model triggers recall()
on 96.3% of evicted-page probes (the mechanism works) but only selects the correct page on
56.6% of those triggered recalls. We call this gap
the bookmark bottleneck. In this section we ask
whether better bookmark generation can close it,
and we report the first systematic study of bookmark generation strategies for cooperative paging.
7.1

Strategies
chunks.paper-memory-paging#39:
We compare six strategies that span the natural design space, from a sanity-check baseline to LLMdriven generation:
• random — four random non-stopword tokens
from the page. Lower-bound baseline.
• heuristic — the surface extractor used in §4:
capitalised multi-character tokens, numerics,
dollar amounts, and dates, filtered against a 60word stopword list.
• tfidf — top tokens by TF·IDF computed over the
pages within the conversation, providing statistical discrimination.
• llm-contextual — one LLM call per page. The
prompt includes a one-line digest of every other
page so the model can pick distinguishing facts.
• llm-batch — a single LLM call covering all
pages at once, with an explicit non-overlap constraint across pages.
• hybrid — start from the heuristic keywords and
use a single LLM call to add one cross-pagediscriminative keyword to each page.
We hold the boundary and eviction policy fixed
at fixed 10 + LRU (k=5 active pages)—a midrange configuration from §5 that ensures meaningful eviction pressure (12 pages on average, ∼58%
evicted) while remaining representative of practical deployments. (The overall best practical configuration fixed 20 + LRU rarely evicts, making bookmark generation differences hard to observe.) The only varying factor is the bookmark

bookmark generation strategy rather than format.
The two successful strategies (hybrid, llm-batch)
are precisely those that preserve the trigger rate
(97.3% and 93.2%) while improving discrimination among already-triggered recalls.
The implication is structural: better bookmarks can only improve cooperative paging if they preserve the model’s incentive
to recall.
Strategies that summarise pages
too informatively—no matter how accurate the
summary—defeat the mechanism.

chunks.paper-memory-paging#44:
selection rule.

Why does hybrid win on synthetic data while
llm-batch wins on LoCoMo? The split is principled, not noise. Synthetic conversations contain
planted facts whose surface forms (allergens, dollar amounts, named contacts) are exactly the targets of the heuristic’s domain extractor; the LLM’s
role is therefore discrimination—adding one keyword that distinguishes near-duplicates while leaving the strong heuristic base intact. LoCoMo conversations contain no such surface anchors: the
heuristic base degenerates into generic chat tokens
(“Dave”, “Wow”), so adding a single discriminative keyword cannot rescue it; the model must
regenerate keywords from scratch under crosspage non-overlap, which is exactly what llm-batch
does.

This suggests a simple selection rule: use hybrid when the heuristic base is informative; use
llm-batch when it is not. A practical proxy is
the average TF·IDF mass of heuristic-extracted
tokens—when this is high, hybrid wins; when
it is low, llm-batch wins. Applied to our two
datasets, this rule yields the best per-dataset strategy and improves average E2E accuracy from
62.5% (heuristic) to 69.0% (+6.5 points).

What we closed and what remains. On real
LoCoMo data, our best strategy raises end-to-end
accuracy from 52.6% to 61.3% and recall precision from 37.7% to 44.4%. This is a meaningful
step but not a complete solution: the remaining
gap to perfect bookmark precision is still large,
and we conclude that bookmark-level changes
alone cannot close it.
Future directions. The structural lesson from

First, query-time reranking: when the model triggers recall, the system can rerank the bookmark
inventory by query-bookmark embedding similarity before resolving the call, which decouples discrimination from generation. Second, multi-stage
recall: the model first picks a coarse topic, the
system narrows to candidate pages, and the model

Take-away. The bookmark bottleneck is real,
partially solvable, and fundamentally constrained
by the information-gap hypothesis. Practitioners
should choose their bookmark generator based on
whether their data exposes distinctive surface tokens; researchers should look beyond bookmark
content for the next factor of improvement.

Why cooperative paging works. LLMs, unlike traditional OS applications, are cooperative
agents: they follow instructions and use tools
when appropriately prompted. Mason (2026) observed that LLMs have incentive to cooperate with
memory management because cleaner context improves output quality. Our bookmark mechanism
exploits this: by providing a lightweight table of
contents for compressed memory, we enable the

be missing. The key insight is that a minimal cue

Bookmark design matters more than mechanism complexity. Our format ablation reveals
a counterintuitive finding: richer bookmarks decrease recall accuracy despite using 3–4× more
tokens. We hypothesize that verbose stubs give the
model a false sense of having sufficient information, reducing tool usage. This suggests that memory management systems should invest in keyword quality (specificity, domain relevance) rather
than keyword quantity. The 25.7pp improvement
from switching generic to domain-specific keywords underscores this: the choice of which keywords to include matters far more than how many
details to pack into each stub.
Page granularity matters more than “smart”
boundaries. The paging design study (§5) produces a related lesson at the structural level.
Content-aware topic shift boundaries—the
natural first instinct—are the worst performing
strategy (56.7%), while coarse fixed-size pages
(fixed 20) achieve 96.7%. The reason is not
that topic detection is bad in principle, but that
bookmarks carry a search cost for the model: every additional bookmark dilutes the model’s attention over the compressed history. Under a tight
context budget, the system should minimize the
bookmark inventory, even at the cost of imperfect
topical coherence within each page.
The bottleneck has shifted to bookmark discrimination. A striking by-product of the paging ablation is that recall() triggering is now

entirely cases where multiple bookmarks share
generic tokens (“budget,” “medical,” a date) and
the model picks one indistinguishable from another. This closes a loop with §6: making keywords more specific is not only a bookmarkformat optimization, but the primary path to further improvement in end-to-end paging quality.

Committed SAE-Feature Traces for Audited-Session
Substitution Detection in Hosted LLMs

Ziyang Liu
Independent Researcher
ziyang.liu.r@outlook.com
chunks.paper-sae-traces#1:
Hosted-LLM providers have a silent-substitution incentive: advertise a stronger
model while serving cheaper replies. Probe-after-return schemes such as SVIP
leave a parallel-serve side-channel, since a dishonest provider can route the verifier’s probe to the advertised model while serving ordinary users from a substitute.
We propose a commit-open protocol that closes this gap. Before any opening
request, the provider commits via a Merkle tree to a per-position sparse-autoencoder
(SAE) feature-trace sketch of its served output at a published probe layer. A
verifier opens random positions, scores them against a public named-circuit probe
library calibrated with cross-backend noise, and decides with a fixed-threshold
joint-consistency z-score rule.
We instantiate the protocol on three backbones—Qwen3-1.7B, Gemma-2-2B, and a
4.5× scale-up to Gemma-2-9B with a 131k-feature SAE. Of 17 attackers spanning
same-family lifts, cross-family substitutes, and rank-≤ 128 adaptive LoRA, all
are rejected at a shared, scale-stable threshold; the same attackers all evade a
matched SVIP-style parallel-serve baseline. A white-box end-to-end attack that
backpropagates through the frozen SAE encoder does not close the margin, and a
feature-forgery attacker that never runs M is bounded in closed form by an intrinsicdimension argument. Commitment adds ≤ 2.1% to forward-only wall-clock at
batch 32.
chunks.paper-sae-traces#3:
A growing share of large-language-model (LLM) inference is delivered through opaque hosted
APIs, and the provider’s quality-for-cost substitution of served models is both profitable and difficult
to detect: a user who pays for access to a 70B-parameter model cannot, from responses alone,
distinguish it from a 7B substitute that happens to answer the specific queries the user sent. Three
lines of work partially address this gap: determinism / verify-rollback re-runs inference bitwise but
does not establish identity; proof-of-inference SNARKs [1] give soundness at 103 –104 × overhead;
response-side fingerprints (LLM MAP [2], instructional fingerprinting [3]) lack a binding primitive.
The closest prior binding primitive is SVIP [4], a secret linear projection of a hidden state returned
on demand; because the projection is requested after service, SVIP admits a trivial parallel-serve
side-channel — the provider serves users from M ′ while answering each verifier query from the
advertised M .
Our contribution. We study a commit-open protocol in which the provider commits, via a Merkle
tree, to the per-position SAE-feature trace sketch of its served sequence at a published probe layer,
before any verifier opening request. Verification checks random openings against a public namedcircuit probe library, calibrated with cross-backend noise, and decides with a fixed-threshold jointconsistency z-score. Within the scoped threat model (Appendix A), a dishonest provider faces three
options: (a) commit from the substitute and be statistically detected, (b) run M to produce the
Preprint.

chunks.paper-sae-traces#8:
instructional fingerprinting [3] recover identity post-hoc from response statistics or planted triggers
with no binding primitive. Gross et al. [7] use mechanistic interpretability for offline behaviour
proofs; we borrow the move of treating MI artifacts as cryptographic payloads but apply it at serving
time and target identity.
Mechanistic interpretability and commit-and-prove. Our probe library is assembled from namedcircuit work: indirect-object identification [8], induction [9], and SAE-backed syntactic/factual
circuits [10–13]. We are the first to use the feature trace as the commitment payload of a verification
scheme. Commit-and-prove SNARKs [1] give cryptographic soundness at 103 –104 × runtime; proofof-useful-work [14] relaxes soundness for compute-as-proof. We occupy an intermediate regime:
the verifier does not prove honest execution, but any non-honest strategy is either detected or pays
honest-service compute (Section 4). Hardware-rooted primitives (Intel TDX [15], NVIDIA H100
confidential computing [16], IMA [17], append-only logs [18, 19]) are orthogonal deployments that
strengthen the Merkle commitment against privileged adversaries rather than substitutes for the
SAE-trace primitive. Table 1 summarises the differentiation.
Concurrent work on auditable inference / fine-tuning. Two recent systems bracket our design.
AFTUNE [20] records auditable execution traces during fine-tuning and inference and spot-checks
them inside a TEE; overhead is 14–83%, and the trust primitive is recomputation rather than a
statistical-structural binding. VFT [21] gives zero-knowledge proofs that a released model derives
from a declared training process (16.8 s/step prover, 4–6 MB proofs); its scope is training provenance,
not per-request serving. We sit between them: an inference-time, sub-millisecond commitment that
does not require TEE hardware, with the binding carried by the per-position SAE-trace sketch and
the probe library rather than by re-execution or ZK circuits. AFTUNE is March 2026 (concurrent
with this submission); both are reported here to position scope, not as baselines (Section 6).

our single-stack serving deployment; we avoid game-theoretic dominance language — strategy (C) is
only 0.97× honest wall-clock on one stack, a deployment-specific cost gap, not a dominance result.

(A) honest: serve y from M , commit its SAE trace.

(B) substitute-serve: serve y from M ′ , commit M ′ ’s trace.

(C) parallel-commit: serve y from M ′ but commit from a parallel M -pass, so openings are consistent with M .

(D) adaptive distillation: fine-tune M ′ under a bounded budget (two evaluated points: publiccorpus φ + r=16 LoRA to 3000 steps; library-aware joint-φ + r=64 LoRA at 1500 steps) to

Parallel-serve closure: commit-open vs. SVIP baseline

To isolate the commit-open binding contribution over probe-after-return schemes, we compare against
a SVIP-style baseline [4] under matched backbone-specific thresholds on 11 attackers across both
backbones (4 Qwen3: cheap lift, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Phi-3.5-mini, rank-64 S TAGE A LoRA; 7 Gemma-22B: 2 same-family lifts, 4 cross-family substitutes, 1 rank-64 adaptive LoRA). In SVIP, an attacker
serving M ′ but retaining read access to open-source M routes the post-hoc probe to M while users
see M ′ — the parallel-serve side-channel. Commit-open binds the SAE trace to the served M ′ before
any probe, so opening is a membership check. Figure 5: SVIP accepts all 11 (11/11 miss, joint-z at
the honest median on both backbones); commit-open rejects all 11 (11/11 detect) at ≥ 2.78 × τpool
(Qwen3) and ≥ 97 × τGemma (Gemma). The gap is the binding step, not stronger attackers (weaker
SVIP variants — probe batching, cached M responses — share the same acceptance envelope,
Appendix W).

Scope. The evidence in this paper covers three backbone–SAE pairs spanning 1.7–9B parameters
(Qwen3-1.7B + transcoder L14, Gemma-2-2B + Gemma-Scope L12, Gemma-2-9B + Gemma-Scope9B L20 width-131k), the adaptation budgets listed in Table 6 (including a rank-128 frontier point on

of parameters and ≥ 70B flagship-class targets remain untested; we rely on the scale-stable threshold
(τ9B =τGemma =1.09, agreement < 10−4 ) as inductive but not conclusive evidence that the primitive
continues to hold at the “70B advertised / 7B served” operating point that motivates the protocol.
Residual uncertainties — SAE/backend drift, MATH-kernel monoculture, session-level FPR under
within-session dependence ρ=0.88, Gemma-σ recalibration, public-probe overfit with 40% mask-flip
sensitivity, r>64/longer-trained/ full-finetune adaptive attackers, a white-box E-E diagnostic that
does not close the margin but does not exhaust the white-box frontier either, and a single-stack rather
than dominance cost argument (the economic binding of strategy (C) is now complemented by the

structural infeasibility of forgery via Prop. 4.2 rather than standing alone) — are enumerated with
evidence pointers and mitigation sketches in Appendix X (Table 15). The scoring rule of Equation (2)
is compatible without protocol change with stronger mitigations including secret-probe rotation, DP
feature sketches, TEE attestation pairing, and an SVIP nonce-after-service redesign, which we leave
to future work.
Broader impacts. The primary positive impact is to increase auditability of hosted LLM serving:
users who currently cannot verify identity gain a binding statistical primitive that is compatible with
existing SAE/transcoder releases. Dual-use risk is limited and asymmetric: the protocol detects
substitution but does not prevent it, and a capable provider could in principle adapt under budgets
beyond those we evaluate. Providers deploying the protocol must be careful not to treat a single
backbone–SAE pair as a backbone-agnostic guarantee; our three-backbone evidence (Qwen3-1.7B,
Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B) argues for the primitive’s transferability and scale-stability up to 9B
parameters, but not for a universal constant across all architectures and model sizes. No humansubject data, model release, or dataset release accompanies this work; the probe library is built from
published named-circuit prompts and the honest pool is synthetic.
chunks.paper-sae-traces#37:
We study a commit-open protocol that binds the provider to the per-position SAE-feature trace of its
served sequence before the verifier’s query, closing the parallel-serve side-channel of probe-afterreturn schemes. Within Table 6, it detects every tested non-adapted substitute at τpool =1.509, holds
the strongest Qwen3 adaptive LoRA at 2.78 × τpool with 1.55× Pile perplexity, separates from
SVIP on 11 attackers across two backbones (11/11 miss vs. 11/11 detect), and transfers to a 4.5×
scale-up — Gemma-2-9B + Gemma-Scope-9B (L20, width-131k) — with a scale-stable threshold
(τ9B =1.09, agreement with 2B < 10−4 ) and cross-family / adaptive-LoRA margins of 260× and
40 × τ9B . Commit adds ≤ 2.1% overhead at batch 32. Priority follow-up: a probe-aware white-box
adaptive-frontier sweep and a DP-rotated secret probe library. Code, probe library, honest-pool
artifacts, and calibration grids will be released upon publication.

virtualization at SmartX, then moved into LLM systems research. He is based in
Singapore, where he started a one-year M.Tech. in Software Engineering at the National
University of Singapore in August 2026. Since September 2026 he has also been building
[FastMM](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666/FastMM), a market-making engine in C++20. He
expects to finish the degree around late August or September 2027. Before that he took a B.Eng. in Software Engineering at the University of
Electronic Science and Technology of China, in Chengdu, graduating June 2024.

[ziyangliu-666](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666), and on
[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ziyangliu666).

His own work, FastMM included, is on GitHub under
[ziyangliu-666](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666).
chunks.about-about#2:
Systems work under a correctness constraint. At SmartX he owned V2V OS, the product
that moves virtual machines off VMware onto SMTX OS — 10,000+ production VMs migrated,
including core financial workloads, which is the kind of deployment where a silent data
corruption is a company-ending event rather than a bug report. The work that follows
from that constraint is unglamorous and specific: idempotent transfer, block-by-block
verification that never blocks switchover, process isolation so one library version
cannot take down a migration, and root-causing guest kernel defects with strace when
the guest is the thing that is broken.
chunks.about-about#3:
The research he moved into carries the same shape. Cooperative memory paging asks what
an LLM actually does when information is missing from its context, and answers it with a
measurement rather than an assumption (it does not reliably signal the gap, and it answers
more confidently without the missing fact). Committed SAE-feature traces make a hosted
model provider prove it served the model it advertised. Copy-as-decode makes an editing
model reference input lines instead of re-emitting them, with a grammar that guarantees
the reference is valid. In each case the interesting part is the guarantee, not the demo.
chunks.about-about#4:
FastMM, the trading engine he builds now, has the same shape. A replay of a recorded session
must send byte-identical orders, and a SHA-256 of both outbound streams checks it. Each
benchmark says what is inside its timed region and what machine ran it. When he found that his
headline latency figure was mostly the benchmark measuring itself, he fixed the benchmark and
published the smaller, honest number.

chunks.about-fastmm#0:
FastMM ([GitHub](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666/FastMM),
[documentation](https://ziy.bio/FastMM/)) is a market-making engine in C++20. Ziyang is its
author. It is his current project, next to the M.Tech. at NUS.

Backtests, replay and live trading run the same strategy code. Strategies are written in
C++ or in Python. Every session is recorded, and a replay of a recording sends the same
orders again, byte for byte. Orders pass pre-trade risk checks before they leave, and the
loss limit trips a kill switch that pulls every quote.

Version 0.2.0 was released on 23 September 2026. It installs without a build:
chunks.about-fastmm#1:
- Python: `pip install "fastmm-engine[hot]"` from [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/fastmm-engine/), wheels for CPython 3.9 to 3.14 on Linux x86-64. The Numba hot hooks need CPython 3.10 or later.
- The C++ programs: a release tarball on GitHub, and the container image `ghcr.io/ziyangliu-666/fastmm`.

Size, counted on 2026-09-24: about 93,000 lines of C++ in `src/` and `include/`, and about
49,000 lines of tests. On 2026-09-23 the default build ran 887 tests, and 955 with every optional codec on. Sixteen design records (ADRs) in
`docs/adr/` give the reason for each large decision.
chunks.about-fastmm#2:
The engine is one template, `Engine<Strategy, Clock, Transport, Feed>`. A live session, a
backtest and a replay use the same engine with different parts:

| Mode | Clock | Feed | Transport |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live | `TscClock` (rdtsc anchored to wall time) | SPSC rings from the network threads | `LiveTransport` |
| Backtest | `SimClock` (virtual time) | in-process events | `SimTransport`: a matching engine and a seeded latency model |
| Replay | `SimClock` | a recorded journal | `ReplayTransport` |

The strategy is a template parameter too. Strategies use CRTP, so the trading thread makes no
virtual calls (ADR-0009).

Hot-path rules, and how each one is enforced:
chunks.about-fastmm#3:
- The trading thread allocates no memory after warm-up. Thirteen test files link a global
  `operator new` that counts calls, and fail on any allocation.
- Hot functions return a result type and throw no exceptions (ADR-0002).
- Prices and quantities are `int64` fixed point at a 1e-8 scale. Products go through
  `__int128`. There is no `double` in price arithmetic (ADR-0001).
- Every message between threads is trivially copyable.

Two threading modes:
chunks.about-fastmm#4:
- `split`, the default: one network thread per venue and one pinned, busy-spinning engine
  thread, joined by single-producer single-consumer rings.
- `single`: one venue's network loop, the engine and the order send all run on one thread.
  No event crosses a core between the packet read and the order write.
chunks.about-fastmm#5:
All numbers below are p50 unless marked. None of them was measured on exchange hardware: the
machines were a WSL2 desktop and two cloud VMs.

| What | p50 | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Tick to order, the engine alone in simulation | 111 to 123 ns (p99 151 to 167 ns) | one pinned core, WSL2 desktop |
| Engine tick to trade, with real network I/O | 2.4 to 2.6 µs | two processes over a veth pair, WSL2 |
| Wire to wire: simulator sends market data, engine's order arrives back | 23.6 to 25.6 µs | same veth setup |
| Wire to wire between two hosts | 278.5 to 344.1 µs, depending on the backend | two Vultr VMs in one cloud VPC |
chunks.about-fastmm#6:
The tick-to-order figure covers one market-data update in: book update, strategy, quote
diff, risk checks, order state and serialisation of the outbound orders. It leaves out the
network, TLS, JSON and the venue. `bench/README.md` states this next to the number.
chunks.about-fastmm#7:
That figure used to read "about 1 microsecond". He found that the benchmark was measuring
itself: about 600 ns of the old figure was Google Benchmark's pause and resume timing, and
170 to 180 ns was a SHA-256 checksum that only the simulator computes. He moved the timing to
`rdtsc` around the timed region only, and took the checksum out of it. Real engine work
came first: running PnL totals replaced a loop over 256 positions in the loss check on every
event, and the engine step went from 9.2 µs to 2.9 µs.

The send path on the veth setup, wire to wire p50:
chunks.about-fastmm#8:
- 47.1 to 55.3 µs before: two `write` calls per order, one order after another, and an
  eventfd wake for each.
- 32.8 to 34.8 µs: one `write` for all orders of one drain of the outbound ring, and no
  eventfd wake when the network thread busy-polls.
- 23.6 to 25.6 µs after the OUCH encoder was fixed. OUCH encode went from 4.40 µs to about
  0.1 µs.

He also measured io_uring for the send. `IORING_OP_SEND` cost the same as `write`. SQPOLL
only moved the send to another core and did not shorten wire to wire, so the prototype was
not kept.
chunks.about-fastmm#9:
He wrote the network stack himself (ADR-0007): an event loop, TLS through OpenSSL memory
BIOs, an RFC 6455 WebSocket client and an HTTP/1.1 client. The event loop has two backends,
epoll and io_uring. The io_uring backend uses the raw system calls, not liburing. On a
loopback TCP echo the two backends measured the same, about 12.8 µs round trip.

Market data for US equities arrives as Nasdaq TotalView-ITCH over UDP multicast
(ADR-0015):

- MoldUDP64 with A/B line arbitration, a reorder buffer, gap re-requests, and a GLIMPSE
  snapshot to join a feed mid-stream.
- An L3 order book per symbol, which feeds an L2 view to the strategies.
- He wrote the ITCH and OUCH 5.0 simulator, `fastmm-sim-itch`, that the engine is measured
  against.
chunks.about-fastmm#10: Three receive backends deliver datagrams through one interface:
chunks.about-fastmm#11:
- `kernel`: batched `recvmmsg`, busy polling, and software and hardware receive timestamps.
  The hardware timestamp path is implemented but was never tested on a NIC that supports it.
- `af_xdp`: kernel bypass through AF_XDP, written on raw `bpf` system calls with no libbpf and
  no BPF compiler. The XDP program is BPF bytecode, assembled in C++. It parses Ethernet,
  VLAN, IPv4 and UDP and redirects only the feed's groups to the socket. Attach falls back
  from native zero-copy to native copy to generic mode. Its tests load the program through
  the kernel verifier and run it with `BPF_PROG_TEST_RUN`. The cloud VMs had no zero-copy
  support, so zero-copy mode was never measured.
- `dpdk`: optional, off by default, DPDK 25.11 built statically.
chunks.about-fastmm#12:
Orders to the Nasdaq simulator can also go out through `user_tcp`, an experimental TCP client
in user space, over AF_XDP or DPDK. It covers the RFC 9293 state machine, retransmission per
RFC 6298, fast retransmit and out-of-order reassembly. It has no SACK and no window scaling.
On the two cloud VMs it cut the host's send cost to a half or a third. The wire-to-wire
differences were inside the VPC's noise, and his own write-up says so.
chunks.about-fastmm#13:
The engine journals every event it consumes, with the engine clock. The journal format,
`.fmj`, is versioned. It holds the instruments, the effective config with the API keys
removed, and the strategy's parameters, then the events in blocks of at most 1 MiB. Each
block carries a CRC32C.

`fastmm-replay --verify` replays a journal and compares the SHA-256 of the recorded outbound
stream with the replayed one. It prints `replay MATCH`, or exits at the first difference.
Operator commands are journaled too, so a session that an operator changed by hand still
replays to the same hash.
chunks.about-fastmm#15:
The kill switch is one atomic word: one bit for the whole engine and one per venue. It trips
on the loss limit, on a full outbound or journal ring, and when every venue is down. A
`kill_file` makes the loss limit a budget for the whole deployment, not for one process: a
restart after a trip refuses to trade until an operator clears it.
chunks.about-fastmm#16:
- **Recovery:** a store records every fill, order, position and kill event. The engine
  hands them to a separate thread through an allocation-free ring. SQLite is the first
  backend. After an outage of the private stream, the engine fetches the fills it missed and
  drops duplicates by execution id. On a restart it restores its position from the store, then
  replays the venue's fills since the last one it recorded. Both need a venue that can return
  past fills, and today only the Binance Spot connector can. Other venues start flat, with a
  warning.
- **Soak test:** a test breaks a live session in five ways, again and again: it drops order
  connections, answers with an HTTP 418 ban, and hides partial and complete fills. Then it
  checks that the position has not drifted.
- **Operator control:** `fastmm-ctl` talks to a running session over a Unix socket. It can
  pull quotes, change a parameter, kill, or flatten. To flatten, the engine sends
  reduce-only IOC orders on a journaled timer.
- **Venue-side safety:** cancel-on-disconnect is armed on Deribit and Binance USDⓈ-M, and is
  available on Bybit.
- **Monitoring:** `fastmm-top` shows a live session and serves a Prometheus `/metrics`
  endpoint. A finished run produces one self-contained HTML report.
chunks.about-fastmm#17:
- Crypto: Binance Spot, Binance USDⓈ-M perpetuals, Bybit and Deribit, over the hand-written
  WebSocket and HTTP stack. The Binance connector can log on once with Ed25519, so each order
  skips its signature. It can also read SBE binary market data: a 20-level depth update
  decodes in 47.6 ns, against 623.5 ns for JSON.
- Equities: Nasdaq ITCH 5.0 market data and OUCH 4.2 and 5.0 order entry.
- Also in the code, behind build options: FIX 4.4, and CME MDP 3.0 generated from CME's SBE
  schema.
chunks.about-fastmm#18:
A Python strategy marks its quoting hooks with `@fastmm.hot`. Numba compiles each hook to a
C function, and the engine thread calls it through a C ABI, without the GIL. Before a hook
is accepted, its LLVM IR is checked against an allowlist that rejects allocation and calls
into the Python runtime (ADR-0013).

Cost per `on_book` call, measured on one core:

| Hook | ns per call |
|---|---|
| The C++ reference strategy | 31.7 |
| The same strategy as a Python hot hook | 36.8 |

Slower model code runs as plain Python on another thread, and publishes parameter updates to
the hooks. `fastmm init my-mm` writes a starter project.
chunks.about-fastmm#19:
Backtests can read Binance's public market data, with the SHA-256 of each file checked. A
backtest reports markouts, fill quality and a PnL decomposition: spread captured, mid drift
after fills, fees and rebates.

He ran the shipped reference strategy on one day of Binance BTCUSDT perpetual (2024-03-27) at
the venue's standard fees. It lost 499.05 USDT on 12,529 fills: the markout was about −0.85
bps at 10 s, and fees were 351.13 USDT. His documentation states the conclusion plainly: the
shipped strategies are reference implementations of published quoting rules, not a trading
edge.
chunks.about-fastmm#20:
A research module measures a signal before a strategy is written around it. On the same day,
book imbalance predicted the next mid move with an information coefficient of 0.580 at
100 ms, falling to 0.060 at one minute.

Shipped strategies: a basic market maker, Avellaneda–Stoikov, and an options market maker
priced with Black-76.

ZIYANG PROTOCOL is a 2D multiplayer extraction shooter. It is live at https://game.ziy.bio/,
and it is the one thing on this list a reader can play rather than read about. The repository
URL still carries the project's old working name; the project is called ZIYANG PROTOCOL.

A round works the way the genre does. Deploy into a map, loot, fight other players and AI,
then hold an extraction point to get out. What is carried out is kept, what is carried in is
lost on death. Between rounds there is a stash, an eight-slot loadout, and a market.

The engineering worth naming is the netcode, and these numbers come from the source, not the
README:
chunks.about-links#8:
- Server and client both tick at 20Hz, and a snapshot goes out every tick.
- The client renders 150ms in the past, interpolating between the two snapshots either side of
  that time, so other players move smoothly instead of teleporting between updates.
- Before judging a hit the server rewinds `RTT / 2 + 150ms`, capped at 500ms, replaying the
  target's position from a 50-entry ring buffer. It samples three points across that window
  rather than one, so a target crossing the bullet's path cannot slip between samples, and it
  rewinds only for human shooters, since AI and turrets already run in the present.
- Snapshot payloads are cut four ways: fields at their default are omitted, the outbound path
  skips Zod so `.parse()` cannot fill them back in, field names are swapped for one or two
  letter short names from a table shipped in the welcome message, and the result is MessagePack
  in a versioned envelope.
chunks.about-links#9:

Visitors ask this, and the honest answer is a fair sample of how Ziyang builds things,
so it is worth answering precisely.

The agent you are talking to runs **in your browser**. Not the UI around a server-side
agent — the harness itself: the tool-calling loop, the retrieval, the sub-agent spawning,
and the event stream this interface renders all execute in your tab. The page is a static
bundle on GitHub Pages; there is no application server.
chunks.about-this-site#1:
One thing cannot live in your browser: the model API key. A public bundle is readable by
anyone, so a key inside it would be extracted and drained. A single edge function holds
the key and does three things — forward a chat completion to DeepSeek, run a web search,
and fetch a URL — while validating that the request is one this site could plausibly have
made. It is a keyholder, not the agent.
chunks.about-this-site#2:
**Retrieval.** The corpus is built ahead of time from his résumé (English and Chinese),
his arXiv preprints, and his own GitHub repositories and pull requests, chunked and indexed
into BM25. The index ships as a JSON file the page fetches on the first question. There
is no vector database and no embedding call at query time: on a corpus this size, lexical
retrieval with the model reformulating its own queries is both cheaper and easier to
debug than a similarity score nobody can read. The tokenizer emits Chinese unigrams and
bigrams, so the Chinese résumé is retrievable rather than one enormous token.
chunks.about-this-site#3:
**Tools.** `retrieve` (BM25 over the corpus), `read_document` (a whole section),
`web_search` and `fetch_url` (through the edge function), `github_activity` (the public
GitHub API, straight from the browser, no key), and `spawn_subagent` — a nested loop with
retrieval-only tools for reading in parallel without filling the main context window.

**What you can see.** Every reasoning step, tool call, argument and result is in the
collapsed activity line above each answer. Open it. The interface reports what the agent
did rather than asserting that it worked, which is the same reason the migration checker
in V2V OS compares disks block by block instead of trusting that the transfer said OK.
chunks.about-this-site#4:
**What is recorded.** The edge function writes one line per question to its runtime log:
the question text, the time, the country the request came from, and a short hash that stands
in for the visitor. The hash is salted with a server-side secret, so it cannot be turned back
into an address by anyone reading the logs. It exists so Ziyang can see what people ask this
page, which is the useful part. No account, no cookie, no analytics script, and no third party
receives any of it.

The design of this interface came from Claude's design tool; the harness behind it was
written for this site.
